AS

The boxed ledge's rail and lid move from poplar to ripped paint-grade ply, and four unspecified fasteners are settled. ledge_front_rail and ledge_lid are 3/4 ply, not 3/4 poplar, each in two pieces with the butt joint at x 53⅛ — the exact centre of ledge_strut[1] (52⅜–53⅞). Neither board could ever have been one piece: the rail is 106¼ and the lid 107, past any sheet or any commonly stocked poplar board, and both faces are painted, so a rip with a stated joint beats a long hardwood board with an unstated one. The rail's joint gets a new member, ledge_rail_splice — 10 × 7¼ of ¾ ply at y 6½–7¼, z 59½–66¾, glued and screwed to both rail pieces from inside the well. It fits the one clear gap in the well's back: ledge_cleat_rail stops at z 59½ and ledge_strut[1] starts at 66¾. The lid needs no splice — it is supported continuously on both long edges, by ledge_cleat and by the rail's top edge, so both ends of its joint line are held. Four fasteners that were UNSPECIFIED or sizeless are now specified. lnd_ledger_rightwall and stringer_c → right wall: ¼ × 4 flat-head structural screws, 2 per stud — a screw crosses 1½ of ledger + ⅝ of drywall = 2⅛ before the stud, so 4 leaves 1⅞ of embedment and 3½ would leave 1⅜. stringer_c's entry had been the bare Rev T phrase “fastens to the right wall”. rear_ledger → bed wall was “lags into every stud” with no size; it is ⅜ × 4, matching lnd_ledger_bedwall. screen_top_plate → slats: adhesive + one #8 × 2½ angled up through each slat into the plate, with 16ga pins to hold it while the adhesive cures. 16ga alone was proposed and is not enough — the structure table calls this screen the guard for a 58 deck and the ceiling note says a 200 lb lean at its top overloads the slat bases, so the top joint is structural. The screen top-plate position is DECIDED at 47¼→50¾ and Drawing 3's 46½→50 + ¾ band alternative is dropped. What settled it is access, not geometry: there is attic space over this ceiling, so blocking can be added between joists wherever the plate lands, and the plate no longer has to be positioned to find a joist. The joist measurement still tells you whether you are screwing to a joist or adding blocking first — it changes the sequence, not the design. Header-to-king straps are scrapped. Both faces of the half wall are sheathed across the header-to-king joint and two continuous top plates bear over the header and both kings; nailed to both, that is a stiffer tie than a strap. Two items stay open and are now stated with their consequence. The deck ply has no fastening to the beam — the joists hang off its face, so the ply's front edge lands at the LVL over eight 10½ gaps — and eight 2×4 blocks would close the diaphragm for one board and 16 screws; recommended, not yet a member. And beam_tongue's note prescribes a ¾ ply cheek over the notch that is not a member at all, so it appears in no takeoff and its y 47½–48¼ position overlaps the deck ply at z 57¼–58. Also: the Rev U header comment that still called the beam's window end and slat 0 “parked” is corrected — both closed at Rev AG. Verify: 0 FAIL, 0 WARN.

The kernel's fan row was comparing two different distances. expected: fan_clearance is a HORIZONTAL reach distance from the platform's finished front face (beam_wrap_face, y 50¾) to the fan disc; the kernel was reporting a true 3D distance to the nearest SLAT and flagging it “differs from expected”. AR

Three lights added under the loft, recessed into loft_ceiling. New loft_lighting key: two 4-inch slim canless LEDs over the desk, sharing one x (12, the true centre of the desk's own depth, x 0-24) and running along y instead — parallel to the window wall and the desk's long axis, at y 12.5 and 37.5 — and one 6-inch over the open floor toward the half-wall at the true midpoint between the desk's inner edge (x 24) and the half-wall's loft face (x 102, clear_below_deck_x): x 63, y 25. Verify: 0 FAIL, 0 WARN. lumber.ply-3/4 already existed for loft_ceiling, so no new stock entry.

A finished ceiling closes the underside of the whole loft. New member loft_ceiling, ¾ ply, x 0→102 by y 0→50 at z 53→53¾ — from the bed wall out to beam_wrap_face, screwed up from below into rear_ledger, side_ledger, every deck_joist and beam, all flush at the 53¾ framing plane. AO

The rear ledger drops to deck level, matching the side ledger. rear_ledger is now a 2×4, not a 2×6 standing 2 proud of the deck — top and bottom both flush with the joists (53¾→57¼). The deck ply now runs over its top to the bed wall instead of butting its face: deck_ply extends from y 1½→48¼ to y 0→48¼, and picks up a bearing connection to rear_ledger (adhesive + #8 x 1-5/8 at 6 o.c., same as the side ledger). This retires ledger_blocking and ledger_blocking_last — they existed only to give the ply's wall-side edge a bearing shelf between joists while the ledger stood taller than the deck; with the ledger and joists now the same depth, the ledger's own top is that shelf, continuously, the whole run. AN

The slats are centred on the beam, not flush with its face. slat moves from y 49¼→50¾ to y 48⅜→49⅞. The centre line is 49⅛, which is the LVL's centre (48¼→50) and the finished beam's (47½→50¾ ) at the same time — the two wrap faces are ¾ each, so both readings of “centred” land on the same line and there was nothing to choose between. This retires Rev T's faces flush with wrap, which had never been more than an ASSUMED reading of that phrase, and it is a deliberate change of look: the screen was one plane with the beam face and is now a grille set ⅞ back on both sides, with a shadow line each side. A quiet structural gain comes with it: a slat used to sit half on the LVL and half on the poplar face wrap, so its screw was centred on ¾ of wood and ¾ of finish; now every slat's ¾ footprint is dead centre over the LVL and the screw with it. Only slat 22 still needs its screw offset, for the unrelated reason that it overhangs the beam's end at x 106¼. Nothing else moves — the top plate keeps its face on 50¾, so the slats are set back from it by the same ⅞.
AM

Three struts across the well, and the lid is decided: never hinged. ledge_strut[0..2] are 2×2s running square to ledge_cleat under the lid, z 66¾→68¼, 5¾ each, from the cleat's face to the back of the front rail. They fix the gap: the rail is a ¾ board cleated only at its foot, and nothing else holds its top on 7¼ — without them the lid-to-rail joint opens or closes along its length. They also back that joint, so the lid lands 1½ × 5¾ on each instead of bridging bare air between its two long edges. The 52⅜ pitch is exact, not round: strut 0 comes flush with the window wall, strut 2 flush with the ledge's stair end at 106¼, and strut 1 lands on the midpoint (centre x 53⅛). The lid is fixed — Rev F's optional hinges are off the table, so every lid fastener is now a countersunk screw rather than a hinge leaf, and the rail-to-lid line is permanent and flush the whole 106¼ rather than something to pull closed at assembly. The consequence to note: the well is a closed void, about 3.5 cu ft. If that storage is still wanted the lid has to be screwed and filled rather than glued, or the box opened from an end.
AL

Rev AK put the front cleat in the wrong place; it goes on the deck. As AK had it, ledge_cleat_rail sat at the top of the front rail as the lid's front bearing — and it was fixed to the rail and to nothing else, so it floated: the whole front of the box still hung off the lid, which is the problem it was meant to solve. It now sits on deck_ply at z 58→59½, y 5¾→7¼, and gives the front rail's bottom edge something to fasten to. The rail is held at both ends now — cleat at the foot, lid at the top — and the lid's front edge fastens straight to the rail's ¾ top edge, no cleat needed there. It is a 2×2, not the 2×4 the bed-wall cleat is, and the reason is the screw: this one is fastened DOWNWARD, so 1½ of cleat plus ¾ of ply lets a 3½ bury 1¼ in a joist, where 3½ of 2×4 on edge would have needed a 6. 1½ is ample to screw a ¾ rail to, and it costs the well 1½ of floor over its bottom 1½ only. Watch the hinges: with the lid tying the rail's top, hinged lids (Rev F left that optional) give that restraint only when closed — a fixed lid, or a stop under its front edge, is the safer choice.
AK

The lid's front edge gets the same cleat its back edge got. ledge_cleat_rail sits behind the top of ledge_front_rail, y 5¾→7¼, top on 68¼ — identical to Rev AJ's ledge_cleat, so the cut list reads 2 off 106¼ 2×4 on edge. Without it the lid's front bearing was the rail's ¾ top edge: half the landing the back has, and a poor thing to screw into. With it the front is 2¼ — 1½ of cleat plus the rail's own ¾ — and the lid is properly carried on both long edges. It earns its keep twice: glued and screwed to the back of the rail over 3½, it stiffens a 10¼ tall ¾ board that is otherwise a thin panel standing on its edge. Screws go in from inside the well, so nothing shows on the face. It narrows the well to 4¼ over the top 3½ only — below 64¾ the well is still the full {ledge_well_w}. Still open: the front rail has no fixing at its base. Nothing ties it to the deck; as modelled the whole front of the box hangs off the lid.
AJ

The ledge lid gets a back bearing. As drawn it was an 8 wide board carried on one edge — the ¾ top of ledge_front_rail — with nothing at all along the bed wall, because rear_ledger's top is at 59¼, nine inches below it. ledge_cleat is a 2×4 on edge against the bed wall, y 0→1½, top on 68¼ = the lid's underside, screwed into every stud. On edge and not flat, so its face is flush with the rear ledger's at y 1½ and the well stays {ledge_well_w} wide — laid flat it would have eaten 2 more. It is also the hinge line, if the lids end up hinged (Rev F left that open). Three connections that were true and undeclared are now declared with it: the lid on the cleat (106¼ × 1½), the lid on the front rail (106¼ × ¾), and the lid on the skirt's top edge at the stair end (¾ × 8, the joint Rev AH reversed). The lid had no connections: row of any kind before this. Cut list: one 106¼ 2×4 — a 10 ft board, or two pieces butted over a stud.
AI

The 2 topper is dropped: the mattress is 8, not 10. mattress.thickness goes 10 → 8 and its top with it, 68 → 66. Sitting headroom comes back to {sitting_headroom}, which is what the change was for — Rev AG had measured mattress + topper together and paid 4 inches of it. Its finished top is still {beam_above_deck} above the deck, which now stands 2½ proud of the mattress instead of ½ — the 1¾ × 14 LVL was sized for the notch and the span, not for a flush line, and 2½ of upstand is a better rail than ½. (2) The boxed ledge comes down to a 3 curb: ledge_front_rail rips to 10¼ (was 11¼, and 7¼ before Rev AG) and ledge_lid tops at 69, not 70. The boxed ledge's lid laps the stair face instead of dying into it. ledge_end_cap — the top of the one skirt board, hw_sheath_stair — stops at 69¼ instead of 70, and ledge_lid runs the full 107 instead of 106¼, out over that edge to the finished face. AG

The beam is a single 1¾ × 14 LVL, notched onto a 2×4 side ledger, and it is the bed rail. Three changes that only work together. (1) The side ledger is a 2×4 at deck level (53¾→57¼), not a 2×10 standing to the beam top. Nothing of it shows above the deck any more: deck_ply runs over it to the window wall (106¼ × 46¾, was 104¾ × 45½) and the boxed ledge's front rail is a plain board — Rev AB's notch and its ledge_front_rail_tongue row are deleted. (2) The beam bears on wood instead of butting it. Rev Z had the beam's end against the ledger's end face on a hanger nobody had chosen. Now deck_joist[0] runs 48½ — past the beam face to y 50, sistered to the ledger over its whole length — and the beam is notched 3 (x) × 3½ (z) out of its bottom left corner and sits on the two of them: 3 × 1¾ = 5.25 sq in of bearing, ~115 psi against 425 allowable, and the kernel measures 2.62 + 2.62. The notch is exactly the d/4 a sawn end notch is allowed and the NDS notch-shear formula gives ≈1,960 lb against a reaction near 600, but LVL makers prohibit bottom notches, so a ¾ ply cheek goes over it on the inboard face. (3) The beam is one 1¾ × 14 LVL, not a doubled 2×10. Depth is set by the mattress, not by load — the mattress is measured now: an 8 mattress with a 2 topper, so its top is at 68 and the beam's finished top at {beam_above_deck} above the deck is ½ proud of it. It is wrapped on three sides — face, bed side and a cap the slats stand on and screw through into the LVL. What moved with them: the LVL's outer face had to stay on 50, so the 1¼ it lost in width went to the joists — they span {deck_joist_span}, not 45½, and the finished bay is {bay} for a 38 mattress ({bay_slack} slack). The slats start at 68½, not 63 — 26 long, was 31½ — and slat 0 is no longer a special case: the beam runs to x 0 under it. beam_end_cap grows to 9¾ and the boxed ledge to 8 × {ledge_h}, an 11¼ rail keeping the lid 2 proud of the mattress the way Rev L intended when the mattress was 6; the stair face is still one board from one 4×8, 50 × 46 now. The price is sitting headroom: 28, was 32 — all of it the mattress, none of it the beam. Three UNSPECIFIED fasteners close (joists to beam, slats to beam, the ledger to the wall) and one opens: FIELD, there must be a stud within 6 of y 50 in the window wall, or blocking added, because the reaction lands 1½–3 off the wall face and the overturning couple now works over 3½ of ledger depth instead of 9¼ — the deck ply glued and screwed to the ledger top is what holds it. In the model: a row may carry part_of, so a notch remnant is checked against the stock it was cut from rather than failing the section check — beam_tongue and deck_joist_tail are the first two, and the kernel fuses each into one solid (the beam is one board, x 0→106¼). verify 0 FAIL, 0 WARN; kernel 111 solids, 0 real interferences. It did find one thing: slat 22 has only ¾ of its 1½ width over the LVL — it overhangs the beam's end onto the stair face — so its screw is offset inboard. Drawings 1, 2, 3, 6 and 7 move. Both audits ran on this rev and both found something. The connection check caught the notch's own pin fastener: it read 2 × ¼ × 4 down through the beam into the ledger, and a 4 in screw started on the LVL's top face at 67¾ dies at 63¾ — 6½ short of the ledger, still inside the beam. It is now 2 × ¼ × 6 driven UP from the open bay below, through the ledger's 3½ into 2½ of LVL, which also fixes the build order: ledger and joist 0 first, drop the beam on, screw from underneath. It also found the half-wall post the beam's note calls “a straight post to the floor” had never been declared — hw_top_plate_2 → hw_top_plate_1 and both kings to their bottom plates are in connections: now, and so is beam_wrap_top → beam, the cap having become structural. slat 22 gets its own row and its own fastener note. The drawing audit found the stair face still stated as 50 × 42 when the ledge cap took it to 50 × 46 (a cut), the revisions card rendering raw {placeholders} because card_revisions() never called fill(), Drawing 7b's view window clipping the beam at 66 so its own dimension pointed at nothing, Drawing 1 omitting beam_tongue and so drawing the beam 3 short of the wall it reaches, and “103 clear span” for what is a centre-to-centre span over a {beam_clear_span} clear one. All fixed. Open: how the 14¾ × 107 face wrap is actually made.
AF

The beam's underside wrap is gone. beam_wrap_underside was a ¾ poplar strip closing the gap between the beam's own underside (53¾) and the face wrap's bottom edge (53) — cosmetic, and it bought the platform ¾ less clearance under the beam than under the joists for no reason anyone could point to. AE

The half-wall's stair face is gone from behind the stair; stringer A lands on the framing. A ¾ ply panel used to run floor-to-58 in the band x 106¼→107, and everything on the stair side stood on it: stringer A, the landing rim, the side member, the bed-wall ledger. It bought nothing — it was a spacer that every fastener had to pass through, and it made the stair's left carriage float ¾ clear of the wall it was screwed to. Now stringer A is at x 106¼→107¾, hard on the half-wall framing, and the landing box moved the same ¾ with it (lnd_side_member 106¼→107¾; lnd_ledger_bedwall and lnd_rim start at 106¼, each ¾ longer). Consequences, in order: (1) stringer A's plumb cut now meets the rim across its full 1½ instead of ¾ of it, and no connection anywhere has a through: path — stringer_a → hw_header drops from a 4½ SDS to a 3½ that buries the same 2 inches, the side member from 5 to 4, and the kernel's ray casts cross 100% material, 0 in air (they crossed 3¾ of 4½ before). (2) One continuous bottom plate on each side: hw_bottom_plate_a and hw_bottom_plate_b now run x 102¾→131 — 28¼ each — absorbing nk_bedwall_plate and nk_shortwall_plate, which are gone. (3) hw_rake_nailer dies straight onto stringer A: its raked end, 1½ × 30 on the slope, is a real glued-and-screwed connection instead of an inch and a half of air behind a panel. (4) What is left of the stair face is a skirt, hw_sheath_stair — one board, where Rev AD needed two. Its bottom edge is a new stair_top rake profile: 48¾ under the landing box and the stringers' top run, then the tread cuts at 40½, 32¼ and 24. With ledge_end_cap and beam_end_cap fused to it, it is 50 × 42 and yields from a single 4×8 (the old face was 50 × 66 and needed two boards). The treads and risers are trimmed back ¾ to butt its face, so the finished stair is still 24 wide and the finished wall face is still x 107 — platform_finished is unmoved. Everything the old panel covered below the skirt line needed no cover at all: y 0→3½ is the nook nailer wall's own bay, y 3½→46½ is the opening and its soffit, y 46½→50 is inside the understair void. (5) Stringer B recentred to 117⅞→119⅜ so the three stringers sit at 11⅝ centres with equal 10⅛ bays; the nook studs, the shortwall struts (still a post under each stringer) and the landing blocking follow. (6) hw_end_cap is one board with a corner cut out — 5 wide above z 24, 3½ below, where stringer A and its skin now pass; the skin follows the stringer out to x 105½→106¼ and runs into that notch at y 50, so the step in a tread's width is 1½ at the wall's end (was ¾) and board 3's notch is 1½ × 5. (7) stringer_a_skin_cleat was a 2×2 touching nothing at either end; it is now a 2×4 on edge, 13½ long, butting the merged shortwall plate at y 50 and ripped to the stringer underside at its far end, dying into the stringer where that line reaches the floor at y 63½. (8) The nook soffit is two boards, nk_soffit_flat and nk_soffit_rake: it was encoded and drawn as a single sheet with a 42.5° kink along it, which is not a thing anyone can cut. They butt on a plumb joint at y {y_meet}, where both faces are on {nook_fin_h} — flush and full-thickness, so the ceiling still reads as one plane turning a corner. Checks: verify 0 FAIL, 0 WARN; kernel 111 solids, 0 real interferences (it caught the first cut of the skirt profile, where Stair.top_edge's tolerance let the tread below win at a run boundary and dropped the panel a whole riser into the stringer). Drawings 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8 and 9 all move.
AD

Both faces of the half-wall are one board each side of one seam, and the nook lining is recessed ¾ behind the face. The nook face was three panels — hw_sheath_loft_a, _head, _b — with the ends of nk_wrap_bedwall, nk_wrap_shortwall and nk_soffit_panel showing between them, because all three lining sheets ran out to x 102 flush with the face: six edges to fill on the surface you meet walking into the nook. Now: the lining stops at x 102¾ (28¼ long, was 29) and the face laps its ends. hw_sheath_loft_head and hw_sheath_loft_b are one board, 45¾ × 53¾, with the opening sawn out of it — its edges moved in from the reveal (3½/46½) to the finished jamb lines (4¼/45¾) and the ¾ offset came off its rake, so its head edge is now the soffit FACE, not the framing line above it. hw_sheath_loft_a is the other board, a 4¼ full-height stile in the bed-wall corner. The one seam falls on y 4¼ — the opening jamb line carried up — and is backed by the wrap end below 41½ and the header above. It is two boards and not one only because the face is 50 × 53¾ and neither dimension fits a 48 sheet; a 5×5 panel makes it one, at the cost of 18 mm ≠ ¾. Nothing inside the nook moved: the lining's faces, the {nook_fin_w} × {nook_fin_h} finished opening and the rake are all as they were, and the face panel's own ¾ edge is simply the first ¾ of each jamb. The stair face is two boards too, and it now caps the ledge and the beam. Piece 1 is hw_sheath_stair_a + a new hw_sheath_stair_a_head + ledge_end_cap — 8 × 66, floor to the top of the boxed ledge in one line, so the joint that ran across at deck level is gone (the end cap changes from ¾ poplar to ¾ ply). Piece 2 is hw_sheath_stair_head (starting at y 8 now) + hw_sheath_stair_b + a new beam_end_cap, 42 × 63 — the beam's stair end was open above the deck, 5 inches of end grain and the 2×10/2×10 seam facing the landing, and the same board now runs up over it. Their seam is on y 8, the boxed ledge's front face, backed by the header, the plates, the deck rim and the deck ply for its whole length.
